Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Before you meet the outlaw, you meet his world. What does a place tell you about who to root for?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
🗺️Setting: I will find Nottingham and Sherwood Forest on a map of England and name when the story takes place.
📖Reading: I will describe the world Robin is born into and point to one detail that shows the law is unfair to the poor.
🔤Words: I will learn the four people words of Robin’s England.
🧵Characters: I will match facts and traits to the people of Chapter 1 and retell the chapter as a tapestry.
📝Writing: I will choose a hero for Quick Write 1 and plan it.

🗺️ Find Robin’s England
The setting: where and when the story happens

The setting is the time and place where a story happens. Start with half of the world, then zoom in. The map of England comes from a history atlas and shows the country about the year 1300, a little more than a hundred years after Robin Hood’s story. The counties and towns had hardly changed.

✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Correct model
In Sherwood Forest, the Sheriff of Nottingham rode out with Prince John.

Every name of one particular person or place starts with a capital letter: Sherwood Forest, Sheriff of Nottingham, Prince John. The plain word forest stays lowercase when it is not part of a name. Use the model to fix the sentence below.

🔧 Fix this one
much the miller lived near sherwood forest, close to the town of nottingham.
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Much the miller lived near Sherwood Forest, close to the town of Nottingham. Four capitals: the first word, the name Much, the place Sherwood Forest, and the town Nottingham. Miller and town name kinds of things, so they stay lowercase.

🪶 Poetry Corner
Listen, then read it aloud yourself.

Green opens Chapter 1 with two lines from this poem. Here are its first three stanzas. You will read the rest of it over the next three lessons.

Alfred Noyes (1880–1958)
0:50
AI voice reading, not a recording of Noyes. Photograph: Bain News Service, Library of Congress, public domain.
A Song of Sherwood
Alfred Noyes (1903) · stanzas 1–3 of 13
Sherwood in the twilight, is Robin Hood awake? Grey and ghostly shadows are gliding through the brake, Shadows of the dappled deer, dreaming of the morn, Dreaming of a shadowy man that winds a shadowy horn. Robin Hood is here again: all his merry thieves Hear a ghostly bugle-note shivering through the leaves, Calling as he used to call, faint and far away, In Sherwood, in Sherwood, about the break of day. Merry, merry England has kissed the lips of June: All the wings of fairyland were here beneath the moon, Like a flight of rose-leaves fluttering in a mist Of opal and ruby and pearl and amethyst.
brake: a thicket of bushes · winds a horn: blows a horn

🔤 Words: The People of Robin’s England
Four of this week’s eight words. Learn them before you read.

These words name where a person stands in a divided society. Say the meaning first, then tap the card to check.

🌾
serf
tap to flip
serf
A poor peasant bound to work a lord’s land, with almost no rights. The Saxon poor are treated as serfs by their Norman lords.
🧑‍🌾
yeoman
tap to flip
yeoman
A free man who farms his own small land, above a serf but below a noble. Robin will build his band from free yeomen.
🛡️
retainers
tap to flip
retainers
The armed servants and followers who serve and protect a lord. The Sheriff keeps armed retainers to enforce his will.
🤴
liege
tap to flip
liege
A lord or king a person owes loyalty to. Robin’s true liege lord is King Richard, even while the king is away.

Professor Lovelore Before you read
1:06
An AI-generated character and voice.
serf noun
A poor farm worker who belonged to a lord’s land. A serf could not leave, had to work the lord’s fields, and had almost no rights.
In our book, the Norman lords treat the Saxons as serfs.
⏸️ Pause in the Prologue

Green says the serfs have “no rights of their own and no chance of real justice.” Why would a writer begin by showing you that the poor cannot get justice?

⏸️ Pause in Chapter 1

Much the miller killed a deer to feed his hungry children. Compare what he did with what the Sheriff means to do to him.

5
📖 Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, Mimic
One sentence from Chapter 1, three ways.
“Robin Hood comes out of the forest – men say he is the Good Spirit of Sherwood – and having brought help, he goes away as silently as he came.”Much, Chapter 1
📖 Read like a Reader

Much says this to Prince John and the Sheriff, who want to know who Robin Hood is. What does Much know about Robin, and what does he not know?

✏️ Read like a Writer

The sentence stops in the middle for a rumor set off by dashes: “men say he is the Good Spirit of Sherwood.” Then it ends on Robin leaving “as silently as he came.” Why break into the sentence with a rumor? What does the ending make Robin seem like?

🖊️ Mimic

Write your own sentence on the same pattern, about anyone or anything.

___ comes out of the ___ – people say ___ – and having ___, goes away as ___ as ___ came.

You have read and noticed. Now bring the people of Chapter 1 to life.

🧵 Stitch the Tapestry
Retell Chapter 1 in four scenes, the way the Bayeux stitchers told their story.

The Bayeux Tapestry tells its story scene by scene, with a short line stitched above each one, and many of those lines begin with the Latin word Hic, “Here.” Build Chapter 1 the same way. For each scene, choose what happens, stitch in the people who are there, and give them words. Type in your own words, then switch to 📜 Olde words to hear them in the voice of the old tales.

🪶 Writer’s Workshop: Quick Write 1, My Hero
Step 1 of 3: choose and plan
1 Plan2 Draft3 Revise
Professor Lovelore In the writer’s room
0:51
An AI-generated character and voice.
Your plan answers three questions
  1. Who is this person, and what did they do? Enough detail that a stranger would understand.
  2. What makes them a hero to you? A specific quality or action, not “they were nice.”
  3. Did they ever break a rule, disobey an authority, or do something others disagreed with? If yes, did that make them more or less heroic?
150–200 words this week · a hero from your own life or thinking, not from the book
📌 Watch how: Ava’s plan

Who: My grandmother, Rosa Delgado, who drove a school bus for 30 years in San Antonio.

What she did: Kept her route running through a flood, house to house, so no kid was left waiting alone.

Quality: Stubborn care. She would not leave anyone behind.

Rule-breaking: Yes. She drove a road the county had closed. I think it made her more heroic, but only because she knew that road better than anyone.

Every line is something you could point to. “Would not leave anyone behind” is stronger than “she cared,” because it names an action. Notice the capitals too: Rosa Delgado and San Antonio are proper nouns.

Who is your hero, and what did he or she do?
The one quality or action that makes them a hero.
Rule-breaking: yes or no, and what you think about it.
